messages.subject: speeding up reading of NCEP data
messages.subject_clean: speeding up reading of NCEP data
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

The micro_ncep function in NicheMapR connects to a global historical dataset of 6-hourly weather conditions. However, those of you who have used it will know that access to it via the RNCEP package is really slow. To speed things up, you could download the NCEP files locally. There is an option for micro_ncep to read local files, if you specify the input 'spatial' as the folder where you've stored the NCEP files.

However, even doing this with the files as downloaded, it is very slow. The reason is that the NetCDF files in which the data is stored have the spatial coordinates specified first, and then the time variable. This means that reading the whole grid of points for one time slice is fast, but reading a whole time series at one location is slow.

This problem can be fixed by reordering the NetCDF file.

I've pasted some R code below that you can use to a) download all the files and b) reorder them. It requires you to have the program NCO  <http://nco.sourceforge.net/>installed on your computer so it can run the program ncpdq  <http://nco.sourceforge.net/nco.html#ncpdq>via a system call (this is what does the rearrangement).

To get the data (replace 'YOUR_LOCATION' with your location, e.g. "C:/NCEP/":

library(curl)
years <- seq(1979,2020)
vars <- c('tmax.2m.gauss.','dswrf.sfc.gauss.', 'prate.sfc.gauss.')
vars <- c('tmax.2m.gauss.','dswrf.sfc.gauss.', 'prate.sfc.gauss.', 'vwnd.10m.gauss.',
  'uwnd.10m.gauss.', 'air.2m.gauss.', 'tmin.2m.gauss.', 'shum.2m.gauss.',
  'pres.sfc.gauss.', 'dlwrf.sfc.gauss.', 'ulwrf.sfc.gauss.', 'tcdc.eatm.gauss.')
for(year in years){
  for(j in 1:length(vars)){
   curl_download(paste0("ftp://ftp.cdc.noaa.gov/Datasets/ncep.reanalysis2/gaussian_grid/",vars[j],year, ".nc"), paste0("YOUR_LOCATION",vars[j],year, ".nc"),quiet=TRUE, mode="wb")
  }
}

To reorder the data (after installing NCO):

library(ncdf4)
dir2do <- "YOUR_LOCATION"
setwd(dir2do)
files<-list.files()
files<-files[grep(".nc", x = files)]
vars4 <- c("tmin", "tmax", "air", "shum", "uwnd", "vwnd")
vars3 <- c("pres", "tcdc", "dswrf", "dlwrf", "ulwrf", "prate")

allvars <- c(vars4, vars3)

for(i in 1:length(files)){
  filenm <- files[i]
  orig <- nc_open(filenm)
  t<-ncvar_get(nc = orig, varid = "time", start = 1, count = -1)

  varid <- names(orig$var)[which(names(orig$var) %in% allvars)]

  if(varid %in% vars3){
    start <- c(1,1,1) # compose the start location vector for getting the data out of the ncdf file for this location
    count <- c(-1,-1,-1) # how much data are wanted? (-1 means all)
  }else{
    start <- c(1,1,1,1) # compose the start location vector for getting the data out of the ncdf file for this location
    count <- c(-1,-1,-1,-1) # how much data are wanted? (-1 means all)
  }

  data <- as.numeric(ncvar_get(orig, varid = varid, start = start, count)) # get the data
  lon<-ncvar_get(nc = orig, varid = "lon", start = 1, count = -1) # longitudes
  lat<-ncvar_get(nc = orig, varid = "lat", start = 1, count = -1) # latitudes
  t2 <- ncdim_def(name = "time", units = " hours since 1800-1-1 00:00:0.0", vals = t, unlim=FALSE) # define a time variable
  lon2 <- ncdim_def(name = "lon", units = "degrees_east", vals = lon, unlim=FALSE) # define a longitude variable
  lat2 <- ncdim_def(name = "lat", units = "degrees_north", vals = lat, unlim=FALSE) # define a latitude variable
  att<-ncatt_get(orig, varid, attname=NA, verbose=FALSE) # get attributes from original file
  if(varid %in% vars4){
    level<-ncvar_get(nc = orig, varid = "level", start = 1, count = -1) # levels
    level2 <- ncdim_def(name = "level", units = "m", vals = level, unlim=FALSE) # define a latitude variable
  }

 if(varid %in% vars3){
    var1 <- ncvar_def(name = varid, units = att$units, dim = list(lon2,lat2,t2), missval = att$missing_value, longname = att$long_name, prec='float') # define the variable
 }else{
    var1 <- ncvar_def(name = varid, units = att$units, dim = list(lon2,lat2,level2,t2), missval = att$missing_value, longname = att$long_name, prec='float') # define the variable
 }

  vars <- list(var1) # get variable definition
  file2<-gsub('.nc', replacement = '_time2.nc <http://time2.nc>', x = filenm) # make a new file name
  file3<-gsub('.nc', replacement = '_time.nc <http://time.nc>', x = filenm) # make a new file name
  ncnew <- nc_create(file2,vars) # create a new ncdf file to put the data in
  ncvar_put(ncnew,var1,data) # put the data in
  nc_close(ncnew) # close the new file
  if(varid %in% vars3){
    cmd<-paste0("ncpdq -a lon,lat,time ",file2," ",file3) # command for ncpdq - permute to reverse order
  }else{
    cmd<-paste0("ncpdq -a lon,lat,level,time ",file2," ",file3) # command for ncpdq - permute to reverse order
  }

  system(cmd) # run ncpdq

  file.remove(file2) # delete the temporary file
}

All the best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hey Mike,

Just to tag on to this conversation, do you have the protocol established yet and/or any way to contribute to the database?  I am primarily interested in salamanders (which honestly seem a bit more complicated in terms of mechanistic modeling) and will be collecting physiology data in the future.  Much of the current work was unfortunately delayed due to COVID-19, but it would be great to standardize future measurements.  I am still unsure how well NicheMapR will work for the salamander species I am working with, especially since I think many of the thermal traits are tied to humidity/VPD, where Tpref, VTmax, etc. would likely vary depending on VPD conditions.  However, with that said it would still be great to contribute to a database with standardized procedures (even if using other modeling approaches).

messages.subject: Ectotherm under different vegetation cover configurations (with DEB model on)
messages.subject_clean: Ectotherm under different vegetation cover configurations (with DEB model on)
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have seen in previous posts that to simulate the vegetation cover I should modify the sun angle, wind factor, besides altering the max/min of shade. However, I want to model the canopy cover and further run the ectotherm model with the DEB model turned on to assess the consequences of different cover configurations (e.g before and after wildfires) on the ectotherm’s life history and physiology.

So my questions are:

Since I am using the DEB model, is the cap parameter (presence of organic matter on the ground) related to the food available for the ectotherm, or it just account for physical properties to model the micro-environments?

By changing the parameter X (food density), does it change the proportion of food that the ectotherm "eats" ?

For comparative purposes, I would also like to compute the average growth rate over a given period (e.g. 5 years). Is there a straightforward way to do that?

Finally, these procedures can be equally applied for the micro_ncep and micro_aust?

Sorry for so many questions. Any suggestion will be highly appreciated.

Thanks,
Rodolfo

messages.subject: Re: Ectotherm under different vegetation cover configurations (with DEB model on)
messages.subject_clean: Ectotherm under different vegetation cover configurations (with DEB model on)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rudolfo,

The 'cap' parameter is altering the thermal properties of the surface as would be the case if there was a reasonable amount of low-conductivity organic matter. I found this was necessary to capture soil temperature in places where there is some vegetation present, e.g. a layer of grass. It's explained further in

Kearney, M. R., Shamakhy, A., Tingley, R., Karoly, D. J., Hoffmann, A. A., Briggs, P. R., & Porter, W. P. (2014). Microclimate modelling at macro scales: a test of a general microclimate model integrated with gridded continental-scale soil and weather data. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 5, 273–286. https://doi.org/doi: 10.1111/2041-210X.12148 <https://doi.org/doi:%2010.1111/2041-210X.12148>
and of course it's in the help files for the microclimate model e.g. ?micro_global
cap = 1, organic cap present on soil surface? (cap has lower conductivity - 0.2 W/mC - and higher specific heat 1920 J/kg-K)
It is completely unrelated to food.
The parameter X is a DEB parameter. It sets the available food but this may be at a level above what is limiting for the animal depending on its maximum foraging rate. I would strongly advise that you avoid using the DEB model without fully understanding what it's doing. It is a steep learning curve for sure but the NicheMapR package hopefully makes learning it easier, because it provides you with something to play with, and there's a vignette about it in the package to get you started but the DEB book is the place to go to properly learn it, and the deblab <https://www.bio.vu.nl/thb/deb/deblab/>.
The outputs of micro_global, micro_ncep, etc. are all identical in structure and the ectotherm model is set up by default to feed in the microclimate data from these runs if you've stored it in a list called 'micro'. So yes, no matter which microclimate function of the 'micro_' style functions in NicheMapR, the ectotherm will run from them. It doesn't make sense to run the DEB model unless you're running a daily time-step. The micro_global function by default runs the middle day of each month so to make that function run daily you'd need to set 'timeinterval' to 365 (and nyears to greater than one if you want to run multiple years).

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: Questions to create rasters with micro_ncep and ectotherm outputs
messages.subject_clean: Questions to create rasters with micro_ncep and ectotherm outputs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Israel,

If you want to generate rasters from the micro_ncep / ectotherm functions, you have to run individual simulations in a loop across a grid (you can parallelise them too) and then summarise the results per location and convert to a raster.

Re the issue of shade, it depends on the organism. You could have no tree cover at a site and yet there could be plenty of shade from bushes, and the shade required depends on the size of the organism.

Also, depending on the question you have, you may not need a super-fine spatial resolution grid but rather a representative set of point simulations.

All the best,
Mike
